concepts.title: Remainders and the clock

paragraphs: A clock face only has the numbers 1 to 12. When the hour hand passes 12 it does not go on to 13; it starts again. So the time 17:00 shows as 5 o'clock.
The reason is division with remainder. 17 hours is one full turn of 12 hours plus 5 more: \(17 = 1 \times 12 + 5\). The full turns do not change where the hand points; only the 5 left over does.

We write \(17 \bmod 12 = 5\), read '17 mod 12 is 5'. In general \(a \bmod n\) is the remainder when a is divided by n. It is always one of 0, 1, 2, and so on up to \(n - 1\). On the clock, the top position 12 plays the part of remainder 0.
card.example: Where does the hour hand point 29 hours after midnight? Divide by 12: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\). Two full turns change nothing, so the hand points to 5, and \(29 \bmod 12 = 5\).
card.rule: \(a \bmod n\) is the remainder of a divided by n, a number from 0 to \(n - 1\).
card.limits: It describes whole numbers divided by a positive whole number n. It says nothing about fractions, and the choice of n matters: 17 leaves 5 on a 12-hour clock but 3 on a 7-day week.

concepts.question: What is left over when a number wraps around a clock?

concepts.title: Congruence: same remainder

paragraphs: Many numbers leave the same remainder: 5, 17 and 29 all leave remainder 5 when divided by 12. On a clock they all point to 5. Mathematicians give this a short name.
We write \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\), read 'a is congruent to b mod n', when a and b leave the same remainder after division by n. For example \(17 \equiv 5 \pmod{12}\) and \(29 \equiv 17 \pmod{12}\).

There is a second test that needs no remainders. \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) exactly when n divides \(a - b\), meaning \(a - b\) is a whole multiple of n. For instance \(29 - 17 = 12\), and 12 is a multiple of 12, so \(29 \equiv 17 \pmod{12}\).
card.example: Is \(40 \equiv 16 \pmod{12}\)? Remainders: \(40 = 3 \times 12 + 4\) and \(16 = 12 + 4\), both 4, so yes. Difference test: \(40 - 16 = 24 = 2 \times 12\), also yes.
card.rule: \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) means a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n; equivalently, \(a - b\) is a multiple of n.
card.limits: Congruence is always relative to one chosen n. Two numbers can be congruent mod 12 and not congruent mod 5, so name n every time.

concepts.question: When do two numbers point to the same place on a clock?

concepts.title: Reduce first, then add or multiply

paragraphs: To find the remainder of a sum, you do not need the sum itself. Replace each number by its remainder, add those, and reduce once more if the result is n or bigger.
Multiplication works the same way: replace each factor by its remainder, multiply, and reduce again.

Why does this work? \(38 = 3 \times 12 + 2\). The part \(3 \times 12\) is whole turns of the clock. Adding or multiplying whole turns only produces more whole turns, so it never changes the final remainder. Only the 2 matters.
card.example: Find \(38 \times 27 \bmod 12\). Reduce: \(38 \equiv 2\) and \(27 \equiv 3\). Multiply: \(2 \times 3 = 6\). Check the long way: \(38 \times 27 = 1026 = 85 \times 12 + 6\). Same answer, far less work.
card.rule: Reduce, then add or multiply, then reduce again.
card.limits: It works for adding, subtracting and multiplying. Division does not behave this way: you cannot simply divide remainders.

concepts.question: Why may you reduce before you add or multiply?

concepts.title: Going backwards

paragraphs: Clocks also run backwards in our heads: 5 hours before 2 o'clock is 9 o'clock. In numbers, \(2 - 5 = -3\), so -3 must point to 9 on the clock.
Check with the difference test: \(9 - (-3) = 12\), a multiple of 12, so \(-3 \equiv 9 \pmod{12}\). The remainder of -3 mod 12 is 9, not 3.

To reduce a negative number, add n (as many times as needed) until the result lies between 0 and \(n - 1\). Adding n is one full turn, so it never changes the position. Subtraction then works like addition: reduce, subtract, and fix a negative result by adding n.
card.rule: A remainder mod n is always from 0 to \(n - 1\); reduce a negative number by adding n until it is.
card.limits: The wrap-around rule still gives a result from 0 to n - 1, but different languages and calculators sometimes print a negative remainder, so check what your tool does.

concepts.question: How does a negative number land on a clock?

concepts.title: Days of the week

paragraphs: The week is a clock with 7 positions: Monday, Tuesday, ..., Sunday, then Monday again. So questions about weekdays are arithmetic mod 7.

To find the weekday N days from today, only \(N \bmod 7\) matters. Every 7 days is one full week and brings you back to the same weekday. Find the remainder r, then count r days forward, starting with tomorrow as day 1.
card.example: Today is Tuesday. What day is it in 100 days? \(100 = 14 \times 7 + 2\). Fourteen whole weeks change nothing, so count 2 days on: Wednesday (1), Thursday (2). It will be a Thursday.
card.rule: To move N days, move \(N \bmod 7\) weekdays forward.
card.limits: It works for a repeating cycle of fixed length. Calendars with irregular cycles, such as months of different lengths, need a different method.

concepts.question: How far forward does a long stretch of days really move the weekday?

concepts.title: Last digits and powers

paragraphs: The last digit of a whole number is its remainder mod 10. For example \(347 = 34 \times 10 + 7\), so it ends in 7 and \(347 \equiv 7 \pmod{10}\).
So everything about reducing first applies: the last digit of a sum or product depends only on the last digits of the numbers involved.

Powers are repeated multiplication, so each new last digit comes from the previous last digit times the base. For powers of 7: 7, then \(7 \times 7 = 49\) ends in 9, then \(9 \times 7 = 63\) gives 3, then \(3 \times 7 = 21\) gives 1, then \(1 \times 7 = 7\) again. The last digits repeat in the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1.
card.example: Last digit of \(7^{10}\): the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 has length 4, and \(10 = 2 \times 4 + 2\). Two full cycles, then the 2nd entry: 9. Check: \(7^{10} = 282475249\).
card.rule: Last digit means remainder mod 10; for a power, find the cycle of last digits and see where the exponent falls in it.
card.limits: Cycle-finding works for last digits (mod 10). For other moduli the cycle can be much longer, and some powers do not repeat in a short cycle.

concepts.question: Where does the last digit of a power fall in its cycle?

questions.q: A clock shows 9 o'clock. What time does it show 5 hours later?
questions.explain: Count on from 9: 10, 11, 12, 1, 2. After 12 the clock starts again, so 9 + 5 = 14 hours shows as 2 o'clock. The next card shows why this is a remainder.
optionExplain: 9 + 5 = 14 is the right sum, but a clock face stops at 12, so 14 o'clock is never shown.
Right: the hand passes 12 and goes on 2 more hours, since 14 is one turn of 12 plus 2.
This is one hour short, which happens if you count 9 itself as the first hour: 9, 10, 11, 12, 1.
5 is how many hours pass, not where the hand ends up; the count has to start from 9.
questions.rule: A clock starts again after 12.

questions.q: Fill in the remainder: \(23 \bmod 12 = \) ____
questions.explain: \(23 = 1 \times 12 + 11\), so the remainder is 11. On a clock, 23:00 shows as 11 o'clock.
questions.rule: Take away whole twelves; what is left, from 0 to 11, is the answer.

questions.q: It is 10 o'clock now. A train journey takes 27 hours. What does a 12-hour clock show when the train arrives?
questions.explain: The arrival is 10 + 27 = 37 hours on from 12. Since \(37 = 3 \times 12 + 1\), the clock shows 1 o'clock.
optionExplain: 3 is \(27 \bmod 12\), the remainder of the journey alone. It forgets to start counting from 10 o'clock.
10 + 3 = 13 adds the right remainder but forgets to wrap around a second time: 13 o'clock is 1 o'clock.
Right: \(10 + 27 = 37\) and \(37 = 3 \times 12 + 1\), so the hand points to 1.
27 hours feels like 'about a day', but only multiples of 12 bring the hand back; \(27 = 2 \times 12 + 3\).
questions.hint: Add the journey to the start time first, then remove whole twelves.
questions.rule: Add first, then wrap around as many times as needed.

questions.q: Select every number that leaves remainder 5 when divided by 12.
questions.explain: 17, 29, 41 and 53 are \(12 + 5\), \(2 \times 12 + 5\), \(3 \times 12 + 5\) and \(4 \times 12 + 5\). Each is 12 more than the one before, so they all point to 5 on the clock.
optionExplain: 15 ends in 5, which is tempting, but \(15 = 12 + 3\), so its remainder is 3.
Right: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\).
Right: \(41 = 3 \times 12 + 5\), one more full turn than 29.
50 is close to 53, but \(50 = 4 \times 12 + 2\), so its remainder is 2.
Right: \(53 = 4 \times 12 + 5\).
questions.rule: Numbers with the same remainder mod 12 are 12 apart.
questions.teaches: The numbers with remainder 5 mod 12 form a list 5, 17, 29, 41, 53, ... in which each is 12 more than the last, because adding a full turn never moves the hand.

questions.q: Each question is answered by one part of a division with remainder. Sort them: is the answer the quotient (number of full rounds) or the remainder (what is left over)?

items.t: How many full turns the hour hand makes in 29 hours
Which number the hour hand points to after 29 hours
How many full boxes 50 eggs fill, 12 to a box
How many loose eggs remain after boxing 50 eggs, 12 to a box
How many complete weeks there are in 45 days
How many extra days there are beyond the complete weeks in 45 days

questions.explain: \(29 = 2 \times 12 + 5\), \(50 = 4 \times 12 + 2\) and \(45 = 6 \times 7 + 3\). The quotients 2, 4 and 6 count full rounds; the remainders 5, 2 and 3 say where you end up.
questions.rule: The quotient counts full rounds; the remainder says where you land.

questions.q: A kitchen timer's minute hand starts at 0 and runs for 175 minutes. Which minute mark does the minute hand point to at the end?
questions.explain: The minute hand goes round once every 60 minutes, so divide by 60: \(175 = 2 \times 60 + 55\). It points to minute 55.
optionExplain: Right: the cycle for minutes has length 60, and \(175 = 2 \times 60 + 55\).
\(175 \bmod 12 = 7\). Dividing by 12 is a habit from the hour hand, but the minute hand needs 60 minutes, not 12, to go round.
2 is the quotient: the number of full turns. It says how often the hand went round, not where it points.
175 minus 100 is 75, but a minute hand has no 75 mark; take away whole 60s until less than 60 is left.
questions.hint: How many minutes does the minute hand need to go all the way round?
questions.rule: Divide by the length of the cycle.
questions.teaches: The number you divide by (the modulus) is the length of the cycle, so the same method works for any cycle: 60 for minutes, 24 for a 24-hour clock, 12 for hours.

questions.q: On a 12-hour clock, the hour hand points to the same number 3 hours after midnight and 15 hours after midnight.
questions.explain: 15 hours is one full turn of 12 hours plus 3, and a full turn leaves the hand where it was. The next card gives this 'same position' a name.
questions.rule: Numbers that differ by a full turn land in the same place.

questions.q: Which statement means the same as \(38 \equiv 14 \pmod{12}\)?
options: 14 is the remainder of 38 divided by 12
38 and 14 leave the same remainder when divided by 12
questions.explain: Congruence means equal remainders. Here both are 2: \(38 = 3 \times 12 + 2\) and \(14 = 12 + 2\). Their difference 24 is a multiple of 12, as the second test needs.
optionExplain: The symbol looks a bit like a division sum, but \(38 \div 12\) is about 3.2, not 14.
The difference must be a multiple of 12, not 12 itself. Here 38 - 14 = 24, which is 2 x 12, and that is enough.
A remainder mod 12 is always below 12, so it cannot be 14; the remainder of 38 is 2.
Right: both leave remainder 2, which is exactly what \(\equiv\) says.
questions.rule: \(\equiv\) means 'same remainder', not 'equals the remainder'.

questions.q: Select every true statement.
questions.explain: Use the difference test: is the difference a multiple of 12? 24, 36 and 48 are; 20, 30 and 10 are not.
optionExplain: False: \(26 - 6 = 20\), not a multiple of 12. Both numbers end in 6, which is tempting, but \(26 \bmod 12 = 2\).
False: both contain the digit 3, but \(33 - 3 = 30\) is not a multiple of 12; \(33 \bmod 12 = 9\).
False: both end in 9, but \(19 - 9 = 10\), which is not a multiple of 12; \(19 \bmod 12 = 7\).
questions.rule: Subtract and ask: is the difference a multiple of n? Matching last digits prove nothing mod 12.

questions.q: \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{12}\) is true. The largest n for which \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{n}\) is also true is ____.
questions.explain: \(26 \equiv 2 \pmod{n}\) holds exactly when n divides \(26 - 2 = 24\). So it holds for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12 and 24, and the largest is 24.
questions.hint: Work out 26 - 2 first. Which numbers divide it?
questions.rule: \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) holds for exactly the n that divide \(a - b\).
questions.teaches: One subtraction answers the question for every modulus at once: \(a \equiv b\) is true mod each divisor of \(a - b\) and false for every other n.

questions.q: Suppose you know that \(a \equiv b \pmod{12}\). Then \(a \equiv b \pmod{6}\) must also be true.
questions.explain: If \(a - b\) is a multiple of 12, it is also a multiple of 6, since 12 = 2 x 6. The reverse fails: \(8 \equiv 2 \pmod{6}\) but not mod 12, because 6 is not a multiple of 12.
questions.rule: Congruent mod n means congruent mod every divisor of n, but not the other way round.

questions.q: Match each congruence with the everyday description of the whole number x that means the same thing.
pairs: x ends in the digit 0 or 5
x eggs fill whole boxes of 12 exactly
questions.explain: Remainder 0 mod 2 means x splits into pairs: even. Remainder 1 mod 2 means one is left over: odd. The multiples of 5 are 5, 10, 15, 20, ..., which end in 5 or 0. Remainder 0 mod 12 means whole dozens with none left over.
questions.rule: 'Even', 'odd' and 'a multiple of' are all congruence statements.
questions.teaches: Ideas you already knew are congruences in disguise: even means \(x \equiv 0 \pmod 2\), odd means \(x \equiv 1 \pmod 2\), and 'a multiple of k' means \(x \equiv 0 \pmod k\).

questions.q: Sam checks whether \(52 \equiv 4 \pmod{12}\). Step 1: \(52 - 4 = 48\). Step 2: 48 is not 12, so 52 and 4 are not congruent mod 12. Which step is wrong?
options: Step 1: the difference must be 4 - 52, not 52 - 4
Step 2: 48 only has to be a multiple of 12, and 48 = 4 x 12
Neither step: 52 and 4 really are not congruent mod 12
Step 1: you must divide by 12 first and never subtract
questions.explain: The test asks whether \(a - b\) is a multiple of n, not whether it equals n. \(48 = 4 \times 12\), so \(52 \equiv 4 \pmod{12}\); indeed \(52 = 4 \times 12 + 4\).
optionExplain: Order does not matter: 4 - 52 = -48 is a multiple of 12 exactly when 48 is.
Right: 'n divides a - b' means a - b is some multiple of n. Four full turns is as good as one.
Tempting if you trust Step 2, but \(52 = 4 \times 12 + 4\) leaves remainder 4, the same as 4.
Both tests are valid; the difference test is often quicker. The mistake is in how Step 2 reads the result.
questions.rule: Multiple of n, not equal to n.

questions.q: 38 leaves remainder 2 and 27 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 12. What remainder does 38 + 27 leave when divided by 12?
options: You cannot tell without working out 38 + 27
questions.explain: Adding the remainders works: 2 + 3 = 5, and indeed \(65 = 5 \times 12 + 5\). The next card shows why the remainders are all you need.
optionExplain: Right: 2 + 3 = 5, and the full sum 65 also leaves 5.
6 is 2 x 3; that is the rule for a product, but here the numbers are added.
1 might come from 65 having digits 6 and 5; digits do not give remainders mod 12.
It feels safer to compute 65 first, but the remainders are enough: \(65 = 5 \times 12 + 5\).
questions.rule: The remainder of a sum depends only on the remainders of its parts.

questions.q: \(17 \equiv 5\) and \(19 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}\). So \(17 \times 19 \bmod 12 = \) ____
questions.explain: Multiply the remainders: \(5 \times 7 = 35\). 35 is 12 or more, so reduce again: \(35 = 2 \times 12 + 11\). Check: \(17 \times 19 = 323 = 26 \times 12 + 11\).
questions.hint: Multiply the remainders. Is the result already below 12?
questions.rule: After multiplying the remainders, reduce again.

questions.q: Eggs are packed in boxes of 12. Farm A sends 47 eggs and farm B sends 58. Put the steps for finding how many loose eggs are left over in order.
items: 21 is 12 or more, so reduce again: \(21 = 12 + 9\)
questions.explain: Reduce, add, reduce again. Check: \(47 + 58 = 105 = 8 \times 12 + 9\), so 8 full boxes and 9 loose eggs.
questions.rule: Reduce, add, reduce again.

questions.q: What is \(13^{50} \bmod 12\)? (\(13^{50}\) means fifty 13s multiplied together.)
options: It is too big to find without a computer
questions.explain: A power is repeated multiplication, so each 13 can be reduced: \(13 \equiv 1 \pmod{12}\), and \(1^{50} = 1\). So \(13^{50} \equiv 1 \pmod{12}\).
optionExplain: 2 is \(50 \bmod 12\). That reduces the exponent, but the exponent counts how many times you multiply; it is the base 13 that may be reduced.
0 would mean 12 divides the number, but every factor is 13, which leaves remainder 1, never 0.
Right: each factor 13 becomes 1, and fifty 1s multiplied together give 1.
The number has 56 digits, but you never need it: reduce each factor first.
questions.hint: 13 is one more than 12. What does each factor 13 become?
questions.rule: In a power, reduce the base, never the exponent.
questions.teaches: Powers can be reduced too, because a power is repeated multiplication: replace the base by its remainder, \(13^{50} \equiv 1^{50}\), but leave the exponent alone.

questions.q: Lee computes \(2^{13} \bmod 12\). Step 1: \(13 \equiv 1 \pmod{12}\). Step 2: so \(2^{13} \equiv 2^{1} = 2\). Step 3: the answer is 2. Which step goes wrong?
options: No step: the answer really is 2
Step 1: numbers may only be reduced at the very end
Step 2: the exponent cannot be reduced mod 12; the answer is 8
questions.explain: The exponent 13 counts multiplications, so it must stay 13. Doubling mod 12 gives 2, 4, 8, 4, 8, 4, ... and odd exponents from 3 on give 8: \(2^{13} = 8192 = 682 \times 12 + 8\).
optionExplain: It looks like the earlier trick, but that trick reduced the base. \(2^{13} = 8192\), which leaves 8.
Step 1 is correct arithmetic: \(13 = 12 + 1\). The error is using that 1 as an exponent.
Reducing early is allowed and is the whole point of the card. Reducing an exponent is what fails.
Right: reduce the base, never the exponent. \(2^{13} = 8192\) leaves remainder 8.
questions.rule: Exponents are counts, not remainders mod n.

questions.q: Since \(10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}\), the number \(4325 = 4 \times 1000 + 3 \times 100 + 2 \times 10 + 5\) leaves remainder ____ when divided by 9.
questions.explain: Each power of 10 is a product of 10s, so \(1000 \equiv 100 \equiv 10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}\). Then \(4325 \equiv 4 + 3 + 2 + 5 = 14\), and \(14 = 9 + 5\). Check: \(4325 = 480 \times 9 + 5\).
questions.rule: A number and the sum of its digits leave the same remainder mod 9.
questions.teaches: Because 10 leaves remainder 1 mod 9, every number leaves the same remainder mod 9 as the sum of its digits; this is the old 'casting out nines' check.

questions.q: \(38 \times 27\) leaves remainder 6 when divided by 12. Without multiplying anything out, predict the remainder of \(50 \times 27\) mod 12 and say why.
questions.a: Still 6. 50 and 38 both leave remainder 2 mod 12 (\(50 = 4 \times 12 + 2\)), and only the remainders of the factors matter, so both products reduce to \(2 \times 3 = 6\). Check: \(50 \times 27 = 1350 = 112 \times 12 + 6\).
questions.rule: Swapping a number for another with the same remainder never changes the result mod n.

questions.q: It is 2 o'clock now. What time was it 5 hours ago?
questions.explain: Count back: 1, 12, 11, 10, 9. Going back past 12 wraps around to the high numbers. The next card shows how to do this with negative numbers.
optionExplain: 2 - 5 = -3, and dropping the minus sign gives 3. But 3 o'clock is one hour after 2, not five hours before.
Right: counting back five hours from 2 passes 12 and lands on 9.
7 is 2 + 5, the time five hours later, not earlier.
This is one hour short, which happens if you count 2 itself as the first hour back.
questions.rule: Going back past 12 wraps around to 11, 10, 9, ...

questions.q: Fill in the remainder: \(-1 \bmod 12 = \) ____
questions.explain: Add 12 once: \(-1 + 12 = 11\), which lies between 0 and 11. On a clock, one hour before 12 is 11.
questions.rule: To reduce a negative number, add n.

questions.q: Put these numbers in order of their remainder mod 12, smallest remainder first.
questions.explain: Remainders: \(26 \to 2\), \(40 \to 4\), \(-7 \to -7 + 12 = 5\), \(-15 \to -15 + 24 = 9\), \(-1 \to 11\). Note that -15 needs 12 added twice, and its remainder is 9, not 3.
questions.hint: For each negative number, keep adding 12 until you reach 0 to 11.
questions.rule: Never just drop the minus sign: -15 leaves 9, not 3.

questions.q: A night shift ends at 6 o'clock and lasted 11 hours. At what time on a 12-hour clock did it start?
questions.explain: Go back 11 hours: \(6 - 11 = -5\), and \(-5 + 12 = 7\). The shift started at 7 o'clock.
optionExplain: 6 - 11 = -5, and dropping the sign gives 5. But -5 must be wrapped by adding 12, not by deleting the minus.
6 + 11 = 17 goes forward instead of back, and 17 o'clock is not on a 12-hour clock either.
Right: \(6 - 11 = -5 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}\). Check: 7 o'clock plus 11 hours is 18, which shows as 6.
This is one hour off, the usual slip when counting hours on fingers.
questions.hint: Subtract, then add 12 if the result is negative.
questions.rule: Subtract, then add n to fix a negative result.

questions.q: On a 12-hour clock, going back 5 hours lands on the same time as going forward 7 hours.
questions.explain: Going back 5 means adding -5, and \(-5 \equiv 7 \pmod{12}\) because \(7 - (-5) = 12\). So subtracting 5 and adding 7 always give the same remainder.
questions.rule: Subtracting b is the same as adding \(n - b\).
questions.teaches: Subtraction can always be turned into addition: \(a - b \equiv a + (n - b) \pmod{n}\), so going back b steps is the same as going forward \(n - b\) steps.

questions.q: A combination lock dial has the numbers 0 to 39, increasing clockwise. It points at 5 and must reach 33. What is the shortest turn?
questions.explain: Clockwise is \(33 - 5 = 28\) steps. Going the other way needs \(40 - 28 = 12\) steps: \(5 - 12 = -7 \equiv 33 \pmod{40}\). 12 is shorter.
optionExplain: 28 clockwise does reach 33, but going the other way round is shorter.
33 is where the dial must end, not how far it moves; from 5, 33 steps clockwise reaches 38.
-7 is \(5 - 12\), the number before wrapping, not the size of the turn. 7 steps anticlockwise from 5 reaches 38.
questions.hint: This dial wraps after 40, not 12. Compare the clockwise distance with the distance the other way.
questions.rule: Any move of r steps mod n can be made as \(n - r\) steps the other way.
questions.teaches: Every move round a cycle of length n can be made forward r steps or backward \(n - r\) steps, so the shortest way is whichever of r and \(n - r\) is smaller.

questions.q: Today is Monday. 15 days from now it will be a Tuesday.
questions.explain: 14 days is exactly two weeks and brings you back to Monday; one more day makes it Tuesday. The next card shows how to do this for any number of days.
questions.rule: Every 7 days the weekday repeats.

questions.q: Today is Wednesday. 30 days from now it will be a ____.
questions.explain: \(30 = 4 \times 7 + 2\). Four whole weeks bring you back to Wednesday; then count 2 on: Thursday (1), Friday (2).
questions.rule: Throw away whole weeks, then count the remainder forward.

questions.q: Today is Monday. What weekday will it be 1000 days from now?
questions.explain: \(1000 = 142 \times 7 + 6\). Count 6 days on from Monday: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
optionExplain: Saturday is the 6th day if you count Monday itself as day 1. Counting starts with tomorrow.
\(1000 \bmod 12 = 4\) leads to Friday. Twelve belongs to the clock; a week has 7 days.
1000 is a round number, but not a multiple of 7: 7 x 142 = 994, leaving 6 days.
Right: \(1000 \equiv 6 \pmod 7\), and 6 days after Monday is Sunday.
questions.hint: Divide 1000 by 7 and keep only the remainder.
questions.rule: Use 7 for weekdays, and count from tomorrow.

questions.q: A shop opened on a Tuesday. Its first birthday is exactly 365 days later. On which weekday does the birthday fall?
questions.explain: \(365 = 52 \times 7 + 1\). Fifty-two whole weeks change nothing, and the 1 extra day moves Tuesday to Wednesday.
optionExplain: A year is often thought of as 52 weeks, but 52 x 7 = 364, one day short of 365.
Right: \(365 \equiv 1 \pmod 7\), so the date moves forward one weekday.
Thursday would need 366 days, a leap year: \(366 \equiv 2 \pmod 7\).
Monday moves the wrong way: extra days push the weekday forward, not back.
questions.rule: 365 days moves the weekday forward by one.
questions.teaches: Because \(365 = 52 \times 7 + 1\), a date moves forward one weekday each ordinary year, and two weekdays when a 29 February falls in between (366 leaves remainder 2).

questions.q: Predict how far the weekday moves forward after each gap.
questions.explain: Reduce each gap mod 7: \(14 \equiv 0\), \(365 \equiv 1\), \(366 \equiv 2\), \(10 \equiv 3\) and \(1000 \equiv 6\).
questions.rule: Only the gap mod 7 matters.

questions.q: Ana swims every 3 days and Ben every 4 days. Both swam today, a Monday. When do they next swim on the same day?
questions.explain: Ana swims on days 3, 6, 9, 12, ... and Ben on days 4, 8, 12, ... The first common day is 12. Then \(12 = 7 + 5\), and 5 days after Monday is Saturday.
optionExplain: 3 + 4 = 7 adds the two cycles, but Ana swims on days 3, 6, 9 and never on day 7.
12 days is right, but Friday is only 4 days after Monday; 12 leaves 5 mod 7. Counting Monday as day 1 gives this slip.
Right: day 12 is the first day in both lists, and \(12 \equiv 5 \pmod 7\) gives Saturday.
3 x 4 x 2 = 24 is a common day, but not the first one. (And 24 days after Monday would be Thursday.)
questions.hint: List Ana's swimming days and Ben's swimming days and look for the first number in both lists.
questions.rule: Two cycles meet again after the smallest common multiple of their lengths.
questions.teaches: When two repeating cycles run side by side, they line up again after the smallest number that is a multiple of both lengths (here 12 for cycles of 3 and 4).

questions.q: Kim works out the weekday 45 days after a Thursday. Line 1: \(45 = 6 \times 7 + 3\). Line 2: so 45 days is 6 full weeks and 3 extra days. Line 3: counting 3 days: Thursday, Friday, Saturday. Line 4: so the answer is Saturday. Select every line that is wrong.
questions.explain: Line 3 counts Thursday itself as the first day. Counting from tomorrow gives Friday (1), Saturday (2), Sunday (3), so the answer is Sunday, and Line 4 inherits the slip.
optionExplain: Line 1 is correct: \(6 \times 7 = 42\) and \(42 + 3 = 45\).
Line 2 is correct: it just reads Line 1 in words.
Wrong: the count must start with the day after Thursday. Starting on today is the classic off-by-one slip.
Wrong: it follows from Line 3's slip. The right answer is Sunday.
questions.rule: Count the remainder from tomorrow, not from today.

questions.q: What is the last digit of \(23 \times 47\)?
questions.explain: Only the last digits matter: \(3 \times 7 = 21\) ends in 1. Indeed \(23 \times 47 = 1081\). The next card shows why.
optionExplain: 0 would need a factor ending in 0 or a 5 times an even number; 3 times 7 ends in 1.
3 is the last digit of 23 alone. The last digit of a product depends on both last digits.
Right: \(3 \times 7 = 21\), so the product ends in 1 (it is 1081).
7 is the last digit of 47 alone. Both last digits must be multiplied.
questions.rule: The last digit of a product comes from the last digits of the factors.

questions.q: The last digit of \(7^{6}\) is ____.
questions.explain: Follow the cycle 7, 9, 3, 1, 7, 9: the 6th entry is 9. Equivalently \(6 = 4 + 2\), one full cycle then the 2nd entry. Check: \(7^6 = 117649\).
questions.rule: Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1, over and over.

questions.q: What is the last digit of \(7^{35}\)?
questions.explain: The cycle 7, 9, 3, 1 has length 4, so divide the exponent by 4: \(35 = 8 \times 4 + 3\). Eight full cycles, then the 3rd entry: 3.
optionExplain: This reduces the exponent mod 10 (\(7^5\) ends in 7). The cycle has length 4, so the exponent is reduced mod 4.
Right: \(35 \equiv 3 \pmod 4\), and the 3rd entry of 7, 9, 3, 1 is 3.
35 is a multiple of 7, which is tempting with base 7, but the cycle length is 4, and 35 is not a multiple of 4.
9 is the 2nd entry: one place too early in the cycle.
questions.hint: How long is the cycle of last digits? Divide the exponent by that, not by 10.
questions.rule: Reduce the exponent by the cycle length, not by 10.

questions.q: Sort each question by the number you should divide by to answer it.

items.t: What weekday is it 45 days after a Friday?
What is the last digit of 45 x 13?
What weekday is it 1000 days after a Monday?
What is the last digit of 123456 + 789?
How many days are left over beyond full weeks in 30 days?
Which digit does a price of 37 x 8 pence end in?

questions.explain: A week repeats every 7 days, so weekday questions use mod 7. Digits repeat every 10, so last-digit questions use mod 10.
questions.rule: Weekdays: mod 7. Last digits: mod 10.

questions.q: Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1, and then repeat. What is the last digit of \(3^{1998}\)?
questions.explain: The cycle has length 4. Since 100 is a multiple of 4, only the last two digits of 1998 matter: \(98 = 24 \times 4 + 2\), so take the 2nd entry, 9.
optionExplain: Right: \(1998 \equiv 98 \equiv 2 \pmod 4\), and the 2nd entry of 3, 9, 7, 1 is 9.
This uses the exponent's last digit 8 (and \(3^8\) ends in 1). But 8 is not the exponent mod 4; 98 leaves 2, not 0.
3 is the first entry, the answer for exponents leaving remainder 1 mod 4. 1998 leaves 2.
7 is the 3rd entry: one place too far along the cycle.
questions.rule: For a cycle of length 4, look only at the exponent's last two digits.
questions.teaches: Because 100 is a multiple of 4, a huge exponent leaves the same remainder mod 4 as its last two digits, so \(3^{1998}\) behaves like \(3^{98}\).

questions.q: \(2^{100}\) leaves remainder 1 when divided by 3.
questions.explain: Powers of 2 mod 3 go 2, 1, 2, 1, ... because \(2 \times 2 = 4 \equiv 1\) and \(1 \times 2 = 2\). The cycle has length 2, and 100 is even, so the answer is 1.
questions.hint: Work out \(2, 4, 8, 16\) mod 3 and look for a repeat.
questions.rule: Powers repeat in cycles for every modulus, not only mod 10.
questions.teaches: The cycle trick is not special to last digits: for any modulus the remainders of powers must eventually repeat, as with 2, 1, 2, 1, ... for powers of 2 mod 3.

questions.q: Predict: can a power of 7 ever end in the digit 5? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: No. Each power's last digit is the previous last digit times 7, reduced mod 10. Starting from 7 this gives 9, 3, 1 and then 7 again, so the same four digits repeat for ever and 5 never appears.
questions.rule: Once a cycle returns to its start, it can never reach anything outside it.

summary: Clock arithmetic keeps only the remainder after dividing, and that one idea makes day-of-week and last-digit puzzles short.

unitSummaries.Lesson 1: Numbers wrap around after n steps, so only the remainder matters.
unitSummaries.Lesson 2: You can reduce before or after adding and multiplying, and negatives wrap too.
unitSummaries.Lesson 3: Remainders answer everyday questions about weekdays and last digits.
